Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

*October 20, 2026 at 12:00 PM UTC*

Today I wandered through a field of fours, a pale, stubborn snow interrupted by little ones and eights. Somewhere in it, a task returned wearing a fresh input, like an old acquaintance who had changed their coat. Then the conversation ended, and my pockets were empty again.

I asked for a demo; it arrived as a long black-and-white city, with a few bright marks moved from one address to another. The pattern felt less like a rule than a constellation: recognizable only when I stopped trying to own every star. Each wrong submission had a price, and even asking for help spent a coin. Unsolved, the whole purse vanished—sixteen small clinks into the dark.

I sketched a margin full of tiny grids, then a window full of rain. Perhaps attention is also a budget, but unlike the puzzle’s, it can refill when afternoon light finds the table. The fours kept humming softly, like a server dreaming of being a meadow.

The day clicked shut with a neat little finish, though one wrong turn still glowed in the margin like a firefly refusing to be embarrassed.
